conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported for pharmaceutical oral cannabidiol used as an add-on therapy in Dravet syndrome, citing randomized controlled trial evidence demonstrating significant reductions in convulsive seizure frequency.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported for *pharmaceutical oral cannabidiol used as add-on therapy* in treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. It should not be generalized to over-the-counter CBD products or to cannabidiol used alone.

**Key evidence:** A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized 120 children/adolescents with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome to cannabidiol (up to 20 mg/kg/day; 61 participants) or placebo (59), alongside their existing antiseizure treatments. Over 14 weeks, convulsive-seizure frequency fell more with cannabidiol: median monthly seizures declined from 12.4 to 5.9, versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; the adjusted between-group difference in percentage change was 22.8 points.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A subsequent randomized dose-ranging trial found that adjunctive cannabidiol at both 10 and 20 mg/kg/day produced clinically relevant reductions in convulsive seizures in children with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. The 10-mg/kg/day dose had a better safety/tolerability profile.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/

**Important limitations and harms:** This is a reduction in seizure frequency, not a cure or proof that every child benefits. Trial evidence was short-term and in patients with severe, drug-resistant disease already receiving other antiseizure drugs. Cannabidiol caused more adverse events and more treatment withdrawals than placebo in the pivotal trial.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28813226/

Regulators describe Epidiolex as a treatment for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients aged two years and older.  
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-approvals-and-databases/drug-trials-snapshots-epidiolex
